title: Stella Mazeika - Turning Classic Games Into Multiplayer Roguelike Experiences
speaker: Stella Mazeika
talk_title: Turning Classic Games Into Multiplayer Roguelike Experiences
description:
This talk is from the 2019 Roguelike Celebration - find out more at https://roguelike.club/event2019.html

Stella is a now graduated Doctor of Computer Science from UCSC; she's now working on Proxi making interesting things out of memories. In her free time, she's a twitch streamer, speedrunner, and randomizer developer/community leader.

chapters.title: What's been Randomized? What hasn't been?

segments.text: STELLA MAZEIKA: So, hi.
Thank you for the introduction.
Let's start this off by talking a little bit more about me because let's face it.
I am Stella.
I am a recovering games academic.
I almost, almost fully out.
I am currently working at kind of an Indy-ish studio.
Details for offline.
By night I am a Twitch streamer, I am a speed runner and I’m a randomizer dev.
It is that last topic that I am really here talking about today.
What is this talk?
We’re going to define and contextualize randomizers, such as that Sonic Adventure
2 rando thing, talk about what is a randomizer, what have we randomized and what context do
we look at these randomizer things in.
And befitting kind of a good talk for the last talk of the day, this is gonna be a Paladin
talk.
My job here is to get you all hyped.
Let's start off by watching this which is me playing the Final Fantasy One randomizer
and not expecting to find that enemy there.
That enemy was randomly placed there by the randomizer.
How many of you are familiar with the original Zelda?
Let's watch this clip.
There I am playing with - wait that sprite looks a little weird.
Why are those enemies there?
Oh, we’re going in here.
Who recognizes the screen?
Who wants to shout-out what happens when I go in there?
Where are we?
AUDIENCE: It’s randomized.
STELLA MAZEIKA: Yes, it is randomized but in the original, or as we say vanilla game,
that is level one.
In this case, no, it has been randomized.
It is level 9.
This is our final dungeon.
This kind of is like that small sampling of experiences we have out of these randomizer
programs.
How they work kind of on a high level is you have some external piece of software be it
something you download or a website.
One of them might look something like this.
You take a ROM and I’m not going to talk about where you got those ROMs, I’m not
allowed to.
You feed it into the program and then you have a series of flags that choose different
settings.
Here you might shuffle around the key items, you might shuffle around what is in the various
treasure chests, you might slide up or down the amount of experience you’re getting
from doing the different enemy encounters in Final Fantasy One.
Then you choose a random seed, which - this is Roguelike, I’m sure you know all about
these, but for those of you who are watching at home and might not be familiar, this is
basically how we choose what particular random choices the generator is going to make.
This is useful if you and your friend want to play the exact same randomized version
of the game.
Then you generate, you load it up into however you want to play these again, ask me about
that offline, and go.
What has been randomized?
Here are some screenshots of a whole bunch of games.
The real answer is here what hasn't been randomized.
The link we have up for the debigare.com/randomizers.
I did a count a few nights ago and there are at least 300 different randomizers on that
list, including the Final Fantasy 4 Roguelikeifyer which I am sure no one here is interested
in.
NES golf.
La-Mulana, which is kind of a - both the new versions of La-Mulana and the original.
Dwarf Fortress has a randomizer, that’s wild.
And shout-out to The Witness.
It has been randomized.
Cool.
So we can randomize a whole bunch of different games.
What things in these games are we even looking at?
For starters we can do aesthetic changes.
As you can see there, the dialogue in that Zelda cave is definitely not what you remember.
Also, Link is not the Zelda sprite in a pink dress, though why not I don't know.
In the FF4 screenshot there, I don’t think Sans Undertale is in FF4.
That's just a sprite swap that happens.
You can randomize enemy skills and locations.
Darknuts in the Zelda overworld is definitely unusual.
Getting your party nuked down by wizards in FF1 is unfortunate but also that was a hilarious
thing that happened.
You can randomize player abilities.
You can procedurally generate maps.
What we have here is the waterfall cave from Final Fantasy 1 as well as the Dragon Warrior
1 overworld.
Just randomly generated maps using interesting feed forward techniques.
And the big thing that gets randomized are these key item locations because these really
effect the space of game.
If you think about a game like Link to the Past, where you have these different items, you
have the hookshot that lets you cross cliffs, you have the power gloves, as you can see
Link grabbing there, that allow you to pick up boulders.
If you shuffle them around, you kind of run into the danger zone.
If you just randomly position these important items that gate different parts of the game
off from different places you can run into situations where, well, I need the flippers
to get the gloves but I need the gloves to get the flippers and the game is no longer
beatable.
The real answer here is that this is where a lot of the time and effort in randomizers
has gone into.
We take a lot of care to place these key items in beatable ways usually by just doing a generate-and-test.
You put all the key items out there.
You make sure that you can get them and if you can't you throw it away, you try it again,
you throw it away, you try again, you throw it away, you try again.
Computers are pretty fast about things.
Recently there have been a few things that have used logic or constraint systems.
The only one I know about is the one I wrote.
If you do that generate and test, generation time can be a bit of a concern if your system
is a little complex, if there are a lot of dependencies, if there are a lot of places
you can put things.
That screenshot was taken at about 10:30 A.M. eastern.
With that out of the way, hey, cool, you know what these things are and, hopefully, you
are excited about them because I know I am.
What context do we view these things as?
They’re games.
They are Roguelikes.
I’m going to stand up here and defend that one.
They are pieces of software.
And they are communities.
As a game, if you play a randomizer, usually you don't think about it as a single playthrough
though that's totally valid.
But a lot of people who play randomizers play through multiple seeds of the same game and
learn and explore both the nuances of the original game and also the nuances that the
randomizer provides.
You have different flag sets if you remember back.
You have a whole bunch of different flags you can turn on and off and sliders you can
tune different parameters on, and so you can build vastly different experiences out of
the feature richness of these randomizers.
You get this sort of meta progression as you go through the games where you get more interesting
base game knowledge such as that Final Fantasy screenshot of Lich being exiled to the fourth
dimension by an instakill spell which you may or may be something you knew about until
you tried it out in a randomizer.
You have randomizer specific knowledge, such as that Fusoya challenge, which is a lot of
text but it’s a particular flag that only exists in the Free Enterprise Final Fantasy
4 randomizer because Fusoya is kind of overpowered otherwise.
You get things like routing.
If I go to this section of the game what items can I get with these sets of items?
And of course things like, we have this particular diagram for doing a glitch in Link to the
Past that allows you to swim in the water without having the flipper item.
So, next, I said randomizers were Roguelikes so obviously I have to quote Wikipedia because
none of you know what a Roguelike is.
According to Wikipedia Roguelike is a subgenre of role-playing video games characterized
by a dudgeon crawl through procedurally generated levels, turn-based gameplay, tile-based graphics,
and permanent death of a main character.
Well, we can eliminate two of these right away because let’s face it, a lot of these
base games are not turn based and don’t not use the tile based graphics.
Does that make them Roguelike-likes?
We have these three bullet points that I do want to address.
You have the notion of the dungeon crawl, you have the procedurally generated levels,
and you have permadeath.
For the dungeon crawl and procedurally generated levels, for some games, yeah no that's pretty
obvious.
We procedurally generated those maps.
But for other games, you get this sort of procedurally generated route through the game.
Oh, I have this item which unlocks this corner of the map which I probably would have gone
to like sixth in the main vanilla version of the game and now I have to piece together
how I am exploring this space to get all the tools I need to beat it.
It’s kind of this weird meta procedurally generated level, in that context.
Additionally, most of the games don't feature permadeath.
A lot of them are RPGs or ARPGs where you die, you respawn, you again.
But in a lot of the randomizer communities one of the big things going on is racing.
You have people sitting down and playing a seed that they know nothing about, they’ve
never seen it before, and they are both playing through it blind to see who can get through
it faster than the other person.
I would argue that in that context, you kind of have a permadeath situation going on where
you die when you stop playing the seed because it’s kind of considered cheating to stop
playing a seed, come back and try to rerun that race again later.
So you have this weird kind of instead of looking at the individual life of the character,
you have this permadeath over the course of an entire run and for the next race you roll
a new seed and try the new layout and generated space again.
Next we have randomizer as a software.
Straight up, these are automated procedural ROM hacking programs.
They are usually external pieces of software from the actual games that go in and transform
the underlying actual game that you’re actually playing into a new thing that you’re playing.
They have known sets of features and make promises about their output.
And finally, and most importantly to me, randomizers are communities.
As we all know, no system can exist in a vacuum.
We require people to go in and play and interact with our software for it to actually have
any existence or meaning.
Communities build around every single one of these randomizers I have encountered, has
a community where people organize to play the game, race each other, teach new people,
host events, get the randomizer promoted and get races of it featured in bigger events.
At the end of the day, software is made out of people and building strong and inclusive
communities around your software is very, very important.
In summary, reminder, this is a Paladin talk, randomizers are awesome.
Randomizers are tools for generating ROM hacks that feature random things that the output
of which you hopefully can't predict.
They are very popular and prolific and more often than not open source.
Every single community I have run into is welcome to new people both on a player and
development side and I double clicked there.
If you are more academic leaning like me they are actually really strong examples of interesting
proc gen in the wild.
So thank you. [Applause]
STELLA MAZEIKA: Are there any questions?
AUDIENCE: One you didn't mention, which I’m surprised by, is the one that mashes Legend
of Zelda Link to the Past and Super Metroid together and switches the items between games
so you have to play through both games to win.
STELLA MAZEIKA: Yes, in fact, you see these combo randomizers, the Super Metroid and Link
to the Past being probably the most well-known one, but they also did one for Zelda 1 and
Metroid 1 as well.
There’s also the notion of multi-world randomizers, which basically take multiple copies of the
same game and shuffle the items around different players where people are playing through network
connected emulators.
I might be running around and I’ll find your hookshot in Link to the Past and now
you have it but it really makes some of the cooperative experience really interesting.
AUDIENCE: Do you think there is like a practical limit to the complexity of these?
I am thinking about a randomized run through of Morrowind and it hurts my head because
there is a lot going on.
STELLA MAZEIKA: Well, I mean, there’s two ways I want to answer that question.
Practical from a player limitation, yes.
A lot of these randomizers do have wacky modes you can get into but most people are going
to take those and dial them back.
I could see a Morrowind randomizer but one that says okay we’re not shuffling everything
everywhere but we are taking the key items and putting those in different locations,
so you have some guarantees about where you need to go or where you don’t need to go.
From a software side, no, I think the sky is the limit.
>> Cool.
Thank you so much.
